text: Metabolic traits and adaptations of mice lacking Slc12a5 in insulin-secreting β-cells. Pancreatic β-cells integrate metabolic and electrical signals to couple nutrient sensing with insulin secretion, yet the physiological contribution of the neuronal K+Cl- cotransporter-2, Kcc2 (Slc12a5) to β-cell function and whole-body metabolic regulation remains incompletely understood. To define its role in vivo, we generated mice lacking Kcc2 selectively in insulin-secreting β-cells (Kcc2βKO) and evaluated growth, body composition, feeding behavior, glucose homeostasis and islet function from weaning through early adulthood. Kcc2βKO mice developed sex- and age-dependent metabolic phenotypes. Females exhibited lower body weight at weaning and increased lean mass during adulthood, whereas males displayed reduced body-weight gain despite increased food intake. Feeding microstructure analyses identified age-dependent alterations in meal patterning in male Kcc2βKO mice. Morphometric analysis demonstrated increased mean islet area without changes in endocrine cell composition, and isolated islets exhibited enhanced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion at younger ages. Male, but not female, Kcc2βKO mice showed improved glucose tolerance and age-dependent differences in glycemic responses to exogenous insulin, whereas both sexes exhibited attenuated glycemic responses to alanine challenge. Fasting blood glucose remained largely preserved across genotypes, although fasting plasma insulin concentrations varied according to sex, age and fasting duration. These findings identify β-cell Kcc2 as a physiological contributor to nutrient-stimulated insulin secretion and demonstrate that disruption of β-cell chloride homeostasis is accompanied by integrated, age- and sex-dependent adaptations in body-weight regulation, feeding behavior and glucose homeostasis.

Gut-targeted interventions to complement PTH-lowering therapy. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a major contributor to skeletal fragility in chronic kidney disease, yet fracture risk remains high despite parathyroid hormone-lowering therapy. In a rat model of chronic kidney disease, Allen et al. showed that combining the prebiotic fiber inulin with a calcimimetic further suppresses elevated bone turnover while improving cortical bone architecture and mechanical properties. These findings highlight the potential of gut-targeted interventions to complement established parathyroid hormone-lowering strategies for improving skeletal health.

Interpreting metabolite associations and proposed biosynthetic routes in Lactiplantibacillus plantarum-fermented Porphyra haitanensis. The recent study by Li et al. links Lactiplantibacillus plantarum fermentation of Porphyra haitanensis with enhanced in vitro lipid-lowering-related activities, metabolomic remodeling, and beverage development. We welcome this integrative approach but suggest that the mechanistic interpretation of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and p-coumaric acid (pCA) should be calibrated to the evidence. Untargeted LC-MS supports fermentation-associated changes in relative abundance, yet metabolite identity and concentration require orthogonal confirmation and targeted quantification. Likewise, accumulation of pCA cannot distinguish de novo synthesis from release of pre-existing phenolics or altered turnover, and neither GABA nor pCA was directly shown to mediate the observed enzyme- or micelle-related effects. The marked rise in pancreatic lipase inhibition after formulation and pasteurization further warrants vehicle and pH-matched controls to exclude matrix effects. We propose targeted validation of metabolite identity, flux, enzyme activity, and compound-specific function to strengthen the proposed biosynthetic and functional links.

Nuclear Receptor Subfamily 1 Group D Member 1 Promotes Wound Healing in Diabetic Mice through Transcriptional Repression of Stimulator of Interferon Genes. Diabetic foot ulcer is one of the most debilitating complications of diabetes mellitus, primarily driven by persistent inflammation and impaired angiogenesis. This study investigates the role of the circadian clock protein, nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group D member 1 (NR1D1), in diabetic wound healing and elucidates its underlying mechanism. Clinical and experimental analyses revealed that NR1D1 levels were significantly reduced in both the serum and cutaneous wounds of diabetic patients and mice, with down-regulated NR1D1 correlating with delayed wound closure. Functionally, NR1D1 knockout markedly exacerbated wound healing impairment in diabetic mice, accompanied by elevated proinflammatory cytokines and dysfunctional angiogenesis. Conversely, NR1D1 overexpression suppressed IL-6 and IL-1β expression and rescued high-glucose-induced vascularization deficits in vitro. Additionally, diminished NR1D1 expression coincided with hyperactivated stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling in both diabetic skin wounds and high-glucose-treated human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Luciferase assays confirmed that NR1D1 directly represses human STING promoter activity. Taken together, the results indicated that NR1D1 deficiency severely deteriorates wound healing by provoking inflammation and dysregulating endothelial angiogenesis, which is driven by the high-glucose-triggered derepression of NR1D1-mediated transcriptional silencing of STING.
